title: Watching Mooloo
whyItMatters: After mastering Recursion/Backtracking (Days 1–2), Simulation (Day 3), Basic Complete Search (Day 4), and Sorting/Sets (Day 5), this problem transitions into Greedy Algorithms & Casework. At each scheduled day dᵢ, Bessie faces a clean local binary choice: extend her existing subscription from dᵢ₋₁ through dᵢ, or let it expire and start a fresh 1-day subscription on dᵢ. Proving why this local greedy choice is globally optimal is a foundational Bronze-to-Silver skill.

paragraphs: Bessie likes to watch shows on Mooloo. Because Bessie is a busy cow, she has planned a schedule for the next N (1 ≤ N ≤ 10⁵) days that she will watch Mooloo. Because Mooloo is a paid subscription service, she now needs to decide how to minimize the amount of money she needs to pay.

Mooloo has an interesting subscription system: it costs d + K (1 ≤ K ≤ 10⁹) moonies to subscribe to Mooloo for d consecutive days. You can start a subscription at any time, and you can start a new subscription as many times as you desire if your current subscription expires. Given this, figure out the minimum amount of moonies Bessie needs to pay to fulfill her schedule.
inputFormat: The first line contains integers N and K.
The second line contains N integers describing the days Bessie will watch Mooloo in strictly increasing order: 1 ≤ d₁ < d₂ < … < dₙ ≤ 10¹⁴.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the minimum total number of moonies Bessie needs to pay so every scheduled day dᵢ is covered by an active subscription.
Note that the large size of integers involved in this problem requires 64-bit integer data types (e.g., "long" in Java, "long long" in C/C++).

additionalSamples.explanation: Bessie buys a 1-day subscription on day 1 for 1 + 3 = 4 moonies, and another 1-day subscription on day 10 for 1 + 3 = 4 moonies, spending 8 moonies in total (cheaper than a 10-day subscription costing 10 + 3 = 13).

sampleExplanation.title: Sample 1 Analysis
sampleExplanation.detail: Bessie buys a single 3-day subscription covering days 7, 8, and 9, spending d + K = 3 + 4 = 7 moonies (cheaper than two separate 1-day subscriptions costing 5 + 5 = 10).

hints.title: Constraint & Cost Structure Analysis
hints.body: Notice that dₙ can be up to 10¹⁴ and K up to 10⁹, so simulating day-by-day is impossible, and you MUST use 64-bit integers (long in Java, long long in C++). Since N ≤ 10⁵ and the days d₁ < d₂ < … < dₙ are already sorted, aim for an O(N) single-pass greedy algorithm.

hints.title: The Local Greedy Decision
hints.body: On the very first day d₁, Bessie must buy a subscription costing 1 + K moonies. For each subsequent day dᵢ (i ≥ 2), compare two options: Option A (Extend) keeps the previous subscription active from dᵢ₋₁ through dᵢ, adding (dᵢ − dᵢ₋₁) days for (dᵢ − dᵢ₋₁) extra moonies; Option B (New Subscription) lets the previous subscription end on dᵢ₋₁ and starts a fresh 1-day subscription on dᵢ for (1 + K) moonies. Simply add min(dᵢ − dᵢ₋₁, 1 + K)! Whether you extended or started fresh, the state going into dᵢ₊₁ is identical (an active subscription ending on day dᵢ), so picking the cheaper local option has zero future penalty.

hints.title: Java / Python Implementation & Edge-Case Tips
hints.body: 64-Bit Overflow (Java/C++): Both dᵢ (up to 10¹⁴) and totalCost (up to ~10¹⁴) overflow 32-bit int! Parse K and every dᵢ with Long.parseLong(...) in Java (or long long in C++) and store totalCost as a 64-bit integer. Standard Fast I/O: Use BufferedReader + StringTokenizer in Java or sys.stdin.read().split() in Python to read N = 10⁵ integers smoothly.

editorial.summary: Start a 1-day subscription on d₁ for 1 + K moonies. For each subsequent scheduled day dᵢ, either extend the current subscription across the gap for (dᵢ − dᵢ₋₁) moonies or buy a new 1-day subscription for (1 + K) moonies — adding min(dᵢ − dᵢ₋₁, 1 + K) to a 64-bit running total.
editorial.complexity: Time: O(N)  |  Space: O(N) (or O(1) streaming)

solutions.python:
import sys

def solve():
    data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.read().split()))
    n, k = data[0], data[1]
    days = data[2:2 + n]
    total = k + 1
    for i in range(1, n):
        extend_cost = days[i] - days[i - 1]
        new_cost = k + 1
        total += min(extend_cost, new_cost)
    print(total)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    solve()
